Article Title: Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang said that he is willing to wait to have kids till Elon Musk’s Neuralink ...
Article Text:
Why Alexandr Wang wants to wait for Neuralink before having kids

Why Alexandr Wang believes children could adapt better

Alexandr Wang, Meta’s AI chief and highest paid employee, has said he is willing to wait to have children until brain-computer interfaces such as Elon Musk’s Neuralink become more advanced. Wang made the comments during an appearance on the Shawn Ryan Show last year while discussing the future of AI, human development and brain-computer interfaces. He said he wants to wait until Neuralink or similar technology “start working” before having kids. “I want to wait to have kids until we figure out how Neuralink or other … start working,” Alexandr Wang said during the podcast.Wang’s reason is linked to how he believes children’s brains could adapt to the technology. During the podcast, he explained that the first several years of a child’s life are an important period for brain development. He argued that the high level of neuroplasticity during childhood could allow children who grow up with brain-computer interfaces to use the technology in ways that adults may not be able to.“In your first like seven years of life, your brain is more neuroplastic than at any other point in your life, like by an order of magnitude,” Wang said.He then compared the idea with how children develop their ability to process information from their senses.Alexandr Wang described a case involving children born with cataracts. He said that if the cataracts prevent a child from seeing during the early years of development, removing them later may not allow the child to develop normal vision because the brain did not learn to process signals from the eyes during the key period.His view is that a similar effect could eventually apply to brain-computer interfaces. “When we get Neuralink and we get these other technologies, kids who are born with them are going to learn how to use them in like, crazy, crazy ways,” Wang said.Wang said a brain-computer interface could eventually become integrated into the way a person's brain works if it is introduced early enough. He believes this could be different for adults who receive an implant later in life.“It'll be a actually like a part of their brain in a way that it'll never be true for an adult who gets like a neural link or whatever, hooked into their brain,” he said.The Meta AI chief also connected his thinking about brain-computer interfaces to the rapid development of artificial intelligence. “I believe a lot in AI,” Wang said, adding that he expects AI to become “smarter and smarter, more and more capable, more and more powerful.”He said AI could eventually take different forms, including robots and other systems.
Article Summary: Alexandr Wang, Meta’s AI chief and highest paid employee, has said he is willing to wait to have children until brain-computer interfaces become more advanced. Wang made the comments during an appearance on the Shawn Ryan Show last year. He said he wants to wait until Neuralink or similar technology “start working” before having kids.

Article Title: Oracle founder Larry Ellison’s first wife filed for divorce 3 months after their daughter's birth; but he was 'determined to remain friends' as ...
Article Text:
Larry Ellison's reflection on the split

Life after the divorce

Oracle founder Larry Ellison faced a personal turning point in 1986 when his first wife, Barbra, filed for divorce just three months after the birth of their daughter, Megan. According to a report by People.com, the split came at a pivotal time in Ellison’s life as he was balancing the early growth of Oracle with the new family responsibilities. Ellison and Boothe, who met while she worked as a receptionist at Relational Software Inc. — the company that would later become Oracle — married in 1983. Their son, David, was born in January of that year, followed three years later by their daughter, Megan, born January 31, 1986.Barbara filed for divorce in April 1986, just three months after Megan's birth, bringing the three-year marriage to an end.In Matthew Symonds' 2003 book "Softwar: An Intimate Portrait of Larry Ellison and Oracle," Ellison said he was determined to remain friends with his ex-wife for the sake of raising healthy, happy children. He also reflected on how fatherhood had reshaped him personally, saying becoming a father fundamentally changed his personality, made him more sensitive to his children's needs and feelings, and gradually made him a more considerate friend and partner more broadly. He described the experience simply as growing up.After the split, Barbara took over the role of primary caregiver, raising David and Megan largely away from the spotlight of Ellison's rapidly growing tech fortune.She instilled in both children an early love of film, reportedly building a collection of more than 3,000 VHS tapes that the siblings would watch repeatedly, including favorites like "Jurassic Park" and "Back to the Future."That shared love of movies would go on to shape both siblings' adult careers. David Ellison founded Skydance Media, the production company behind franchises including "Mission: Impossible" and "Top Gun: Maverick." Megan Ellison founded Annapurna Pictures, which has produced acclaimed films such as "Zero Dark Thirty," "Her," and "American Hustle," earning her multiple Academy Award nominations along the way.Ellison, now one of the world’s wealthiest individuals, has been married and divorced multiple times.
Article Summary: Oracle founder Larry Ellison faced a personal turning point in 1986 when his first wife, Barbra, filed for divorce just three months after the birth of their daughter, Megan. Ellison and Boothe, who met while she worked as a receptionist at Relational Software Inc. — the company that would later become Oracle — married in 1983.

Article Title: Jamie Dimon and his wife, Judith, donate $12 million to 12 Black colleges and universities; the gift establishes ...
Article Text:
JPMorgan CEO Ja​mie Dimon

Jamie Dimon Foundation gives $12 million to 12 HBCUs

Benedict College in Columbia, South Carolina

Dillard University in New Orleans

Edward Waters University in Jacksonville, Florida

Huston-Tillotson University in Austin, Texas

Jarvis Christian University in Hawkins, Texas

Johnson C. Smith University in Charlotte, North Carolina

Miles College in Fairfield, Alabama

Oakwood University in Huntsville, Alabama

Shaw University in Raleigh, North Carolina

Stillman College in Tuscaloosa, Alabama

Tuskegee University in Tuskegee, Alabama

Voorhees University in Denmark, South Carolina

Jamie and Judith Dimon have backed education initiatives earlier

JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon and his wife, Judith, have donated $12 million to 12 historically Black colleges and universities in the US through their foundation. The gift establishes the Dimon Fund to Advance Economic Opportunity and forms part of the United Negro College Fund’s (UNCF) $1.5 billion capital campaign. Announced by UNCF, the donation will provide permanent endowment capital to the 12 selected institutions. The foundation’s contribution will be paired with $5 million in institutional matches from UNCF’s pooled endowment fund.In a joint statement reported by Fortune, Jamie and Judith Dimon said: Our system of HBCUs continue to serve as the springboard to success for thousands of students in pursuit of the American Dream. As the children of first-generation high school and college graduates, we were imbued with a thirst for knowledge and a drive to succeed principles that we have passed on to our own children and that we wish to share with all the students at the selected HBCUs. ”The latest $12 million donation is directed specifically toward 12 HBCUs. Rather than being used solely for short-term programs, the money will go toward permanent endowments at the schools, the report noted.UNCF said the structure is intended to give the institutions funding that can support their work over a longer period.The 12 HBCUs receiving funding from the Dimon Foundation include:UNCF said it selected the 12 institutions based on their leadership and their records of preparing students for fields including teaching, nursing, and other health care professions. The organisation said these are high-demand areas in which HBCUs have a significant role in preparing first-generation college students.The James and Judith K. Dimon Foundation has been supporting initiatives involving education and economic mobility since 1996. While the foundation does not maintain its own website, public tax records seen by ProPublica show that it paid out more than $9 million to various organisations in 2024, including groups focused on public schools and career development. Its work has also included initiatives to connect students with career opportunities.The HBCU donation follows other education-related work associated with the Dimon Foundation. Judith Dimon, the foundation’s president, oversees grantmaking focused in part on career-connected learning for public school students in New York City.The foundation also helped launch FutureReadyNYC, an initiative that aims to provide 100,000 students with hands-on career experience by 2030. The program is focused on giving students exposure to careers and opportunities before they complete high school. Jamie Dimon has also previously served on UNCF’s board.
Article Summary: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon and his wife, Judith, have donated $12 million to 12 historically Black colleges and universities in the US. The gift establishes the Dimon Fund to Advance Economic Opportunity and forms part of the United Negro College Fund’s $1.5 billion capital campaign. The donation will provide permanent endowment capital to the 12 selected institutions.

Article Title: Apple CEO John Ternus first-ever memo to employees as CEO also has a 'message' on iPhone 18 series
Article Text:
Leadership restructuring at Apple

Read Apple CEO John Ternus ’s first memo to employees here

Team,

Today, on my first day as CEO, I just wanted to send a quick note to thank everyone for the warm wishes. I also want to extend my deep appreciation to Tim for sharing so much of his knowledge and experience during this transition, and more importantly, for everything he contributed to Apple over the years.

We're so lucky to have had a CEO who led with his values and with such decency and humanity. We are all better for it, and I'm so grateful he'll be our executive chairman.

I'm honored to be stepping into this role at what is truly the greatest company in the world, and I am so excited about everything we have in store. We have a huge launch next week that's going to be phenomenal. Thanks for everything you've all done to make it possible.

I'm just as excited about what lies beyond that, including the incredible products already in the works and the ones we haven't even imagined yet that we'll dream up and create together. There's no team in the world I'd rather build the future with.

More to come. In the meantime, thanks for your excellent work!

John

Ternus is a longtime Apple employee, having first joined the company in 2001. Prior to becoming CEO, he was senior vice president of Hardware Engineering, so he has a product-focused background instead of the operations background Cook has.

Apple's leadership team has been reorganizing during the transition from Cook to Ternus, and the full effect of the changes will play out over the next several years.

Johny Srouji is now Apple's chief hardware officer, taking over the Hardware Engineering team that Ternus previously led. Former engineering VP and Ternus lieutenant Laura Legros is returning to Apple, and the product design team was restructured.

On his last day as CEO, Cook told employees he took "enormous comfort" in handing leadership of Apple to "someone as brilliant and wonderful and capable as John."

Ternus has been on stage during Apple events before, but the September 9 "Surprise and Shine" iPhone event will be his first as Apple CEO.

John Ternus has officially stepped into the role of Apple CEO today (September 2), with Tim Cook transitioning to Executive Chair. According to a report by MacRumours, in his first memo to employees, Ternus praised Cook’s leadership, calling him a CEO who led with “values, decency, and humanity. ” He expressed gratitude for Cook’s guidance during the transition and said Apple is “so lucky” to have him continue as executive chairman.In the memo, Ternus described Apple as “the greatest company in the world” and thanked employees for their support. He emphasized his excitement about Apple’s future and highlighted the company’s upcoming launch event next week, which he said will be “phenomenal.” Ternus also gave a subtle nod to the iPhone 18 series, expected to debut at Apple’s September 9 “Surprise and Shine” event. He wrote: “I’m just as excited about what lies beyond that, including the incredible products already in the works and the ones we haven’t even imagined yet that we’ll dream up and create together. ”Ternus, who joined Apple in 2001 and previously served as Senior Vice President of Hardware Engineering, brings a product-focused background to the CEO role. As part of the leadership transition:* Johny Srouji has been named Chief Hardware Officer.* Laura Legros, a former engineering VP, is returning to Apple.* The product design team has been restructured.
Article Summary: Apple CEO John Ternus sent a memo to employees on his first day in the role. He thanked Tim Cook for his guidance during the transition and said Apple is "so lucky" to have him continue as executive chairman. In the memo, he also highlighted the company's upcoming launch event, which he said will be "phenomenal"

Article Title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang joins the list of CEOs who disagree with Bill Gates warning on AI; says: Don’t forget ...
Article Text:
Jensen Huang, CEO, Nvidia.

Jensen Huang says AI will change jobs, not end work

Nvidia CEO sees a boom in skilled trade jobs

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is pushing back against the growing warning that AI could leave millions of people without jobs. While Microsoft cofounder Bill Gates has warned that AI could eventually cause massive unemployment, Jensen Huang says the technology will also create a huge number of new jobs. “Don’t forget the chip plants that are being created—packaging, computer plants, and all of the AI factories being created—hundreds of thousands of jobs are being created as we speak,” Huang said on Fox Business last week.The Nvidia chief believes the AI boom will not simply remove jobs. Instead, he expects the nature of work to change, while demand grows for workers needed to build the infrastructure powering the technology.During the interaction, Jensen Huang acknowledged that some jobs will disappear as AI becomes more capable. But he said history shows that major technological advances also create new types of work.“Everybody’s job changes,” Huang said. “Some jobs will be eliminated. Many new jobs will be created. If you go back and look at history and technology, revolutionary technology comes along, incredible advances come along.”Jensen Huang’s comments come after Gates warned that the impact of AI on employment could be much larger than many people expect. Huang, however, remains optimistic about the future of work. He also believes traditional white-collar jobs will continue to exist, while the growing AI infrastructure industry could create major opportunities in skilled trades.Jensen Huang has repeatedly highlighted electricians, plumbers, carpenters and other skilled workers as some of the people who could benefit from the AI boom. “Having a large population of skilled labor and people who build things, that make things with their hands, is tremendous for the United States,” the 63-year-old Nvidia CEO said.Huang previously said that the skilled trades could see a major boom because of the number of new factories and data centers being built.“If you’re an electrician, you’re a plumber, a carpenter—we’re going to need hundreds of thousands of them to build all of these factories,” Huang told Channel 4 News in the UK in September 2025. “The skilled craft segment of every economy is going to see a boom. You’re going to have to be doubling and doubling and doubling every single year.”
Article Summary: Jensen Huang says AI will change jobs, not end work. Microsoft cofounder Bill Gates has warned that AI could eventually cause massive unemployment. Huang believes traditional white-collar jobs will continue to exist, while the growing AI infrastructure industry could create major opportunities in skilled trades.

Employees to make pre-tax payroll contributions to their children's Trump Accounts through employer cafeteria plans.

Michael Dell's $6.25 billion pledge

The announcement comes months after Dell Technologies founder Michael Dell and his wife Susan Dell pledged $6.25 billion to Trump Accounts through the Michael & Susan Dell Foundation to support the child savings initiative, one of the largest commitments made to the programme. Announcing the new update, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said: “Trump Accounts are giving American families a new way to build wealth from day one”.The new Treasury guidance allows employers to make tax-free contributions of up to $2,500 a year for employees' dependent children and lets workers contribute pre-tax money directly from their paychecks into their children's Trump Accounts. The Michael & Susan Dell Foundation said it would use the funds to help launch the child savings programme, then known as Trump Accounts and later renamed Invest America Accounts. The donation is intended to provide $250 to the accounts of 25 million American children when the programme begins, making it the foundation's largest-ever philanthropic commitment.The Treasury's latest guidance is expected to make it easier for employers to participate in the programme that the Dell Foundation has backed financially.According to the Treasury Department, more than 50 companies have already committed to making Trump Account contributions for employees' children. The department said this means even children who do not qualify for the government's $1,000 Treasury seed contribution can still receive tax-free employer contributions into their accounts.The Treasury also said the programme gives businesses "a new, low-cost, tax-preferred benefit" that can help attract and retain workers while helping families save for the future.To establish a Trump Account employer contribution program, the employer must:

Article Title: Apple's new CEO John Ternus gets a $58 million pay package, and there's a condition that iPhone-maker has to…
Article Text:
Apple's new CEO John Ternus gets $55 million in stock, but most of it pays out only if Apple beats the S&P 500.

Apple has to beat the S&P 500 before most of John Ternus's pay lands

Tim Cook stays on, and the gap between his pay and his successor's is small

Ternus was promoted for products, and products are what he has to prove on September 9

Apple has told regulators what it will cost to run Apple. John Ternus , who became chief executive on Tuesday, gets a $3 million annual base salary and a stock award targeted at $55 million for fiscal 2027, which puts his package at roughly $58 million. There is also a one-time prorated grant of restricted stock units worth about $2.5 million, covering the months of fiscal 2026 he spends in the chair.What makes the number interesting is how little of it is guaranteed. Three-quarters of that $55 million is performance stock, and it vests only if Apple's total shareholder return beats the rest of the S&P 500. Keep pace with the index and the largest part of the new CEO's pay never arrives. Bloomberg, which went through the SEC filing first, reported that Apple has stayed quiet on what the two men could earn in cash bonuses on top of all this.The remaining quarter of the annual award is time-based, vesting semiannually at 12.5 per cent a time over four years. None of these figures are fixed, because the value tracks Apple's share price from here. At a market value of about $4.7 trillion, a few percentage points of drift against the index move the arithmetic by millions in either direction.Cook, who ran Apple for 15 years, becomes executive chairman with a $2 million salary from September 26 and a targeted equity award of $45 million, which comes to about $47 million. His conditions are gentler too, with only half the stock tied to S&P 500 performance against Ternus's three-quarters. For scale, Cook's 2025 compensation was $74.3 million, and he holds more than three million Apple shares, which makes the salary line close to a rounding error.Ternus, 51, led hardware engineering across every Apple product line before moving up, so the promotion reads as a bet on execution rather than strategy. He inherits the job a week before the annual iPhone launch, where a foldable iPhone is expected alongside refreshed Apple Watch and AirPods models, and a wider rollout of the rebuilt Siri that Apple needs to land after a year of falling behind. His first note to staff promised "a huge launch next week that's going to be phenomenal. "Cook keeps the diplomacy, including Washington and Beijing. Ternus keeps the products, and collects most of his $58 million only if investors decide Apple is worth more than the market average.
Article Summary: Apple's new CEO John Ternus gets $55 million in stock, but most of it pays out only if Apple beats the S&P 500. Tim Cook, who ran Apple for 15 years, becomes executive chairman with a $2 million salary from September 26.

Article Title: Google’s ad tech empire stays intact: Here is what the judge ordered
Article Text:
Google ad tech business remains intact

Court rejects Justice Department’s call for asset sales

In a major legal victory for Google-parent Alphabet, a federal judge has decided that Google will not be forced to dismantle its advertising technology operations, sparing the search giant from the government's antitrust remedy. Presiding over the case in the US District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia, Judge Leonie M. Brinkema filed her decision under seal, previewing the core outcome through a brief court order.Notably, Judge Brinkema concluded last year that Google violated federal antitrust statutes to defend its grip on the automated infrastructure that delivers web display advertisements. However, in the final judgement, she stopped short of ordering structural divestitures.The ruling marks a pivotal rejection of the Department of Justice's (DoJ) core enforcement demand. The government prosecutors argued that compelling Google to spin off key components of its ad tech portfolio was essential to restore competition across the digital advertising market. But as per the Judge’s order, rather than mandating a corporate breakup, Google is directed to alter its internal business practices to level the playing field for rival firms.The decision leaves Google's commercial foundation intact just as the company accelerates capital expenditures in the AI sector. Despite losing two historic federal antitrust suits: one covering online search and the other covering ad tech tools, courts have refrained from imposing major structural breakups on the tech titan.Meanwhile, Google continues to advance against emerging AI developers such as Anthropic and OpenAI. The company has integrated generative AI tools across core platforms like search while channeling billions of dollars into high-capacity data centers.The Virginia decision signals ongoing difficulties for federal regulators seeking to break up Big Tech conglomerates, as per The New York Times. Following a separate ruling that found Google held an unlawful monopoly in general search, industry critics condemned that judge’s eventual corrective measures as toothless.
Article Summary: Court rejects Justice Department’s call for asset sales. Judge Brinkema concluded last year that Google violated federal antitrust statutes to defend its grip on the automated infrastructure that delivers web display advertisements. However, in the final judgement, she stopped short of ordering structural divestitures.

Article Title: Google launches Gemini 3.8 Flash and Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber, claims model beats Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol on some benchmarks
Article Text:
Gemini 3.8 Flash: High-end reasoning at low cost

Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber : Automated vulnerability detection and patching

Google has officially introduced two models under Gemini 3.8, calling it the company's strongest coding and logical reasoning model to date as the company continues a rapid deployment cycle that marks its third Flash launch in six weeks. The latest models arrive three weeks after the debut of version 3.7 Flash, the new release matches the high processing speeds and low cost of its predecessor while branching out into two distinct editions: a general-purpose workhorse model and a specialised cybersecurity release.According to Google, both these models share a common intelligent foundation strengthened by iterative training in cybersecurity, enhanced by recursive agentic loops that continually assess and sharpen performance.Designed for complex, multi-stage reasoning, software development, and autonomous agent workflows, the standard Gemini 3.8 Flash delivers a major step up from version 3.7 while keeping initial pricing fixed at $0.75 per million input tokens and $3.75 per million output tokens, Google says.“Today we’re introducing a new 3.8 Flash model, our 3rd Flash release in just 6 wks. It delivers significant leaps from 3.7 Flash across software engineering, agentic tasks, and multi-step reasoning.On DeepSWE v1.1, it outperforms most larger frontier models in autonomously solving complex engineering problems end to end, at a fraction of the cost,” said CEO Sundar Pichai in a post on X.As per the company, Gemini 3.8 Flash managed to surpass most larger frontier AI systems at a much lower cost on the DeepSWE v1.1 evaluation test, which measures end-to-end software engineering capabilities over extended tasks.The second variant, Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber, is tailored directly for defensive digital security teams and is being distributed to verified defenders through Google's newly unveiled Fairwind Program. Google emphasised that development for the Cyber model focused heavily on vulnerability remediation rather than offensive exploitation techniques.“We’re also introducing Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber, our most capable cybersecurity model. It shows frontier-level performance in discovering vulnerabilities and patching them at scale, with Flash-level speed & pricing. That includes achieving 86.2% on the important CyberGym industry benchmark, plus 47.2% on CWE-Bench for patching. We saw a 70%+ success rate in discovering vulnerabilities across 20 programming languages on our internal benchmark,” Pichai said in a separate post.On the same benchmarks, Anthropic’s Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol scored 83.8% and 83.6%, respectively.Google says it has already integrated Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber into active production defenses. Testing by Google's Chrome Security division revealed that the model generated 2.6 times more accurate vulnerability patches for the Chrome browser than the top commercial models of much larger scale.“Beyond benchmarks, we’re seeing impressive real-world use cases. For example, in evaluations on real Chrome security bugs, 3.8 Flash Cyber produced 2.6x more correct patches for vulnerabilities than larger models. Because of its advanced capabilities, we're giving Government agencies & cybersecurity partners access through the Fairwind program,” Pichai added.
Article Summary: Google has officially introduced two models under Gemini 3.8, calling it the company's strongest coding and logical reasoning model to date. The latest models arrive three weeks after the debut of version 3.7 Flash. The new release matches the high processing speeds and low cost of its predecessor while branching out into two distinct editions: a workhorse model and a specialised cybersecurity release.

Article Title: Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora to companies investing in AI: You cannot get your millions of investment right till you buy ...
Article Text:
‘The $1 trillion modernisation mandate’

Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora has said that enterprises pouring capital into artificial intelligence (AI) must urgently modernise approximately $1 trillion in aging digital defenses designed for an earlier technological era because the legacy protection systems put in place seven to ten years ago are fundamentally incapable of countering modern digital threats automated operating at machine speed. He emphasised that businesses cannot successfully roll out AI without establishing proper cybersecurity first.During the company’s post-earnings investor call, Arora highlighted a massive technological shortfall facing global enterprises. Malicious actors are increasingly using automated systems to discover and exploit security gaps faster than ever, leaving older infrastructure vulnerable to instant breaches. Arora told CNBC that global companies carry around $1 trillion in outdated cybersecurity debt that must be overhauled to withstand automated, high-velocity attacks.Arora recalled that nine months ago, the industry was widely written off on assumptions that AI would eliminate its core business. He identified the debut of Anthropic’s Mythos system earlier this year as a decisive industry turning point.“Nine months ago, ... we were guilty and convicted of near death because AI was going to eat our lunch, breakfast, and dinner.It seems like that’s not the case. It seems like we’re going to have to have the feast with them,” Arora said.“I’ve been trying for eight years to tell customers they’re not ready, and [Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei] did it in one event, just by launching Mythos,” Arora said on CNBC.Arora noted that enterprise budgets will not shift overnight. “Not everything’s going to happen next quarter. But all I say is this changes the long-term growth rate and duration of cybersecurity, not just for Palo Alto, but as an industry,” Arora added.
Article Summary: Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora said enterprises must urgently modernise $1 trillion in aging digital defenses designed for an earlier technological era. Malicious actors are increasingly using automated systems to discover and exploit security gaps faster than ever, leaving older infrastructure vulnerable to instant breaches.

Article Title: Two of America's biggest AI companies are in price war, and the links go to China
Article Text:
Cuts for mid-tier AI models

Corporate budgets drive adoption of Chinese silicon

OpenAI and Anthropic – two of America’s artificial intelligence (AI) pioneers – have slashed access fees for their language models to stop budget-focused enterprise clients from migrating overseas even as they face mounting pressure from low-cost Chinese rivals. The price battle arrives as mounting computing expenses force corporations across Europe and Silicon Valley to curb their usage. This has allowed Chinese developers like DeepSeek and Moonshot to win over major business accounts.Citing Silicon Data’s token price index, the Financial Times reported that rates paid by consumers for flagship US models have plummeted nearly 25% since mid-July. The downward shift highlights a pivot for domestic developers, who long relied on proprietary, closed architectures and competed primarily on raw technical power rather than pricing.The recent US developer price cuts are mainly on intermediate products, which are designed to be as economical as open-weight alternatives. OpenAI has cut the price of access to its fastest and cheapest option, GPT-5.6 Luna, by 80%. Input token rates plummeted from $1 down to $0.20 per million, while output charges dropped from $6 to $1.20 per million.Similarly, Anthropic launched Claude Opus 5 at $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output tokens, offering top-tier reasoning at exactly half the rate of its premium Fable 5 tier.Additionally, the startup abandoned a price hike on its Sonnet 5 model that was scheduled for September.The pricing battle unfolds as both Anthropic and OpenAI prepare for initial public offerings (IPOs) at trillion-dollar valuations, all while institutional backers demand clear paths to profit on massive infrastructure expenditures.Simultaneously, both US providers have moved business clients away from flat-rate subscription agreements toward usage-based billing, charging enterprises directly for the computing power they utilise. In response to rising overhead, commercial customers such as Airbnb and DoorDash have started deploying Chinese-built models to contain operational expenses.These decisions coincide with rapid advancements from Chinese labs, which have sharply narrowed the technical performance gap against top-tier American systems while allowing developers to freely download, run, and modify their model weights.
Article Summary: OpenAI and Anthropic have slashed access fees for their language models to stop budget-focused enterprise clients from migrating overseas. The price battle arrives as mounting computing expenses force corporations across Europe and Silicon Valley to curb their usage. This has allowed Chinese developers like DeepSeek and Moonshot to win over major business accounts.

Article Title: Uber layoffs: Company cuts 3,300 jobs; CEO Dara Khosrowshahi says, "I realize this is a lot of change, but it was better to…
Article Text:
Uber cuts 3,300 jobs, 10% of its global workforce.

Uber's job cuts target managers and micro-teams, not just headcount

Uber's restructuring brings remote roles down to about 1 percent of staff

Robotaxi spending explains the timing behind Uber's layoffs

Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi 's email to employees, in full:

Team,

Today, we're making a number of significant organizational changes across Uber. We are removing layers, simplifying team structures, refining our global location strategy, and focusing our people and investments against the biggest opportunities ahead of us. As a result, we will be reducing the size of our team by about 10%. Everyone whose role has been affected has already been notified, except in countries where we will follow the required local process.

This wasn't a decision we made lightly, because it will have a real impact on our teammates and friends who have worked hard for Uber. It's important to say that these changes are about how we're organized and what we're prioritizing, not about anyone's contributions to Uber, which we will always value.

I'm sure you're asking, 'Why, and why now?'—particularly since our business is performing so well. Over the last 5+ years, Uber has grown by orders of magnitude, with our top line nearly tripling.

We've built new products, expanded into new businesses, reached more consumers and supported more earners, and become a much larger and stronger company. But that growth has also brought complexity: more layers, more coordination, more fragmented ownership, and in some cases structures that made sense when businesses were smaller but no longer serve us well at our current scale.

Our opportunity from here is enormous: we have the chance to bring Uber to hundreds of millions more people; to invest even more in drivers, couriers and merchants; and to innovate across our core businesses and build the autonomous future.

To do those things, we need to make deliberate choices about where we put our people, our time, and our capital.

The changes we're making today are designed to do two things: make Uber simpler and faster, and create more capacity to invest in our future. A leaner organization will mean clearer ownership, faster decisions, and more time spent building rather than coordinating. It will also generate savings that we intend to reinvest in growth, innovation, and the capabilities that will matter most over the coming years.

It's our job as leaders to make these difficult calls, and to give you transparency into our thinking and our decision-making process. Here's what we are doing and why:

Organizational health: In Pulse surveys and conversations with many of you, we've heard that too much work requires coordination across teams, debates take too long, and decision-making rights are unclear. I'm sure many of you have felt that you spend too much time "aligning" rather than building, shipping, or serving customers. To improve this, we have reduced roles primarily focused on coordination, and have clarified the remit of the coordination roles that remain. We also cut down the number of management layers by broadening manager scopes, particularly where we had "micro-teams" of only 1-2 reports. In all, we've reduced the number of employees who sit 7+ layers from the CEO by 20% and the number of micro-teams by nearly 50%. The outcome is a simpler org chart geared toward building versus managing.

Team simplification: We brought together teams where fragmentation was creating duplication and slowing decisions. The most significant example of this is Mac's decision to combine our three current Delivery Ops teams (across Restaurants, Retail, and Direct) into single-threaded teams at the global, regional, and country levels. Running these three businesses separately made sense in their early days, but that structure is no longer serving us at scale. Bringing the P&Ls together under single owners will reduce overlap, clarify accountability, and allow GMs to allocate capital more efficiently and effectively based on their strategic imperatives. Another example of this: in Tech, we're combining our Core Services Engineering and Science teams, mirroring the structure we already have on Mobility and Delivery.

Location strategy: The benefits of sitting together, collaborating in person, and solving problems as a team are clearer than ever in our post-Covid world. With that in mind, we're establishing clearer principles for where roles and teams should be based, with the goal of concentrating teams in a smaller number of key hubs. Global teams will be concentrated in our largest global hubs, NY and SF; regional teams in designated regional hubs; local teams in country hubs; and tech teams in tech hubs. We'll prioritize co-location between managers and their teams wherever possible, particularly for earlier-career employees. We are also asking the vast majority of remote employees to move to an office, and going forward, only ~1% of employees will be remote. We'll also continue to reinforce compliance with our hybrid work policy, which requires three days a week in the office.

I realize this is a lot of change, but we decided it was better to make one big shift rather than multiple small ones. We also know organizational changes can be hugely distracting, and our job is to create an environment that allows you to focus and do your best work.

With these decisions now made, our focus is on the future.

We have tremendous momentum, significant financial capacity, and opportunities in front of us that are larger than at any point since I joined the company. The decisions we're making today are difficult, but they will help us build an even stronger Uber for the years ahead.

You can read more about the changes across the company here, and please be sure to read specific follow-up information you'll receive from your leaders about what this means for your team, so we can all keep building together.

Uber on,

Dara

Uber is cutting about 3,300 jobs, close to 10 percent of its global workforce, in the sharpest restructuring the ride-hailing company has attempted since the pandemic. The layoffs were announced on Wednesday in a companywide email from chief executive Dara Khosrowshahi , who framed the decision as a fix for an organisation that had grown too many layers between the people making calls and the people building products. Everyone affected has already been told, except in countries where local labour rules require a longer process.The scale is easier to grasp with the older numbers next to it. Uber had roughly 34,000 employees at the end of last year. After this round, headcount drops to just under 30,000, which is about where the company stood in 2021. The last time Uber cut deeper was May 2020, when it let go of about 6,700 people as lockdowns wiped out ride demand. This time the business is doing well, and Khosrowshahi said as much in the email, which is exactly why the announcement landed the way it did.The restructuring is aimed at the shape of the org chart rather than any single division. The number of managers falls by 20 percent, with some moved into individual contributor roles instead of being let go. Uber also reduced the count of employees sitting seven or more reporting layers below the CEO by 20 percent, and cut "micro-teams" of only one or two reports by nearly half.Non-managers are affected too.Teams are being merged where the company felt the split had stopped making sense. The three delivery operations groups covering restaurants, retail and Uber's white-label direct service are being folded into single-owner teams at global, regional and country level. In tech, Core Services Engineering and Science are being combined, mirroring how Mobility and Delivery are already run.The other significant change is where people sit. Global teams will be concentrated in New York and San Francisco, regional teams in designated regional hubs, and tech teams in tech hubs. Most remote employees are being asked to move to an office. Going forward only about 1 percent of staff will be fully remote. The existing three-day-a-week hybrid policy stays in place, and Khosrowshahi said compliance with it will be reinforced.Khosrowshahi said the savings will be reinvested in growth and in what he called the autonomous future. That is not an abstract line. Uber has committed more than $10 billion to robotaxi partnerships over the coming years and has been reshuffling capital to fund it, trimming stakes in some companies while investing in Avride, Lucid, Nuro and Rivian.The pressure is visible in the stock. Uber shares have fallen nearly 8 percent this year and lagged the S&P 500, with investors worried that Waymo and others could chip away at Uber's North American lead. The stock rose about 2 percent in premarket trade after Wednesday's announcement.One detail sets this apart from most tech layoffs of the past two years. Khosrowshahi did not blame artificial intelligence anywhere in the email, even though the company has been steadily pushing AI into daily operations. The cuts follow smaller reductions in customer service and human resources earlier this year, and a May decision to slow hiring.
Article Summary: Uber is cutting 3,300 jobs, 10% of its global workforce. CEO Dara Khosrowshahi: "These changes are about how we're organized and what we're prioritizing" Uber's restructuring brings remote roles down to about 1 percent of its workforce.

Article Title: Meta 'junks' Google for Salesforce's Slack as it thinks that Google Chat is not good for…
Article Text:
Meta is switching its internal chat from Google Chat to Slack this month, with AI agents driving the decision.

Alexandr Wang told staff the second switch in a year will be disruptive and painful

Salesforce picks up a high-profile Slack customer as it pushes AI agents

Meta is moving its internal communications from Google Chat to Slack later this month, with chief AI officer Alexandr Wang telling employees the switch is being made because Slack handles AI agents better. Wang laid out the reasoning in a memo sent on Monday, which Business Insider reported on, citing Slack's conversational interface for agents, its developer tooling and its third-party integrations.The decision reverses a call Meta made less than a year ago. Wang said that when the company first compared the two platforms, they looked similar on features, and leadership went with Google Chat because it worked with Google Workspace. "In retrospect, we made the wrong decision," Wang wrote, saying AI had evolved considerably since then and that it was increasingly clear how fundamental agents would be to how Meta builds.Wang acknowledged in the memo that another migration so soon would be hard on employees, describing it as disruptive and painful. He said the leadership team still believes Slack's stronger agentic capabilities justify the effort, and that while not everyone at Meta is building agents right now, the whole company stands to gain from a working agent ecosystem.The rollout happens in two phases. Meta Superintelligence Labs, the Agent Transformation Accelerator and DevInfra get early access from September 15.The rest of the company follows on September 29. A Meta spokesperson declined to comment. Salesforce also declined, and Google did not respond to a request for comment.The move is a win for Salesforce, which bought Slack for $27.7 billion in 2021 and has spent the last two years building agent features into it, including a one-click route to deploy agents built on outside platforms such as LangChain, n8n, Lovable and OpenAI.Salesforce stock has fallen over the past year on doubts about whether AI agents will eventually displace the software people pay for. The shares rose nearly 23 per cent in a single day last week after an expanded partnership with Anthropic and results showing growth in new annual orders.
Article Summary: Alexandr Wang told staff the second switch in a year will be disruptive and painful. He cited Slack's conversational interface for agents, its developer tooling and its third-party integrations. The move is a win for Salesforce, which bought Slack for $27.7 billion in 2021.

Article Title: Elon Musk responds to Apple CEO John Ternus' 'Hello' message
Article Text:
AMD CEO Lisa Su , Salesforce chief Marc Benioff extend congrats to new Apple CEO

Apple’s leadership transition after 15-year Tim Cook era

Billionaire Elon Musk , and multiple other tech executives have extended their congratulations to newly-appointed Apple CEO John Ternus, reacting directly to the executive’s first-ever post on social media platform X (formerly Twitter). Making his first public post on the platform since stepping into Apple ’s top leadership role, Ternus shared a minimalist greeting that read simply, “hello”.Responding to the update, the Tesla and X chief wrote, “Congrats!"”before following up with an additional comment noting, “New Apple CEO posting on X”.Not just Musk, executives including AMD CEO Lisa Su, Salesforce chief Mac Benioff, Logan Kilpatrick , who is the product lead for Google AI Studio, also wished the new Apple CEO.“Congrats John! All the best,” said Su. Benioff added a simple “Congrats” with a heart emoji. Kilpatrick said: “good morning.” IBM posted a meme in which a person is seen waving hand in “hello” fashion.Tech millionaire Bryan Johnson posted a long message, welcoming Ternus on X, saying, “Hey John, congratulations and welcome to X.”“A heads up that you may see some unusual things from me on the TL. I'm trying to stop. Also, I see you were an accomplished rower at Penn.lmk if you want to join me in an attempt to dunk a basketball. We're the same age,” he added.Greg Joswiak, Apple SVP marketing replied to Ternus post: "Hello, indeed. More to say September 9. 😉"Ternus formally stepped into the chief executive seat on September 1, 2026, marking the conclusion of Tim Cook’s 15-year tenure leading the technology giant. The 51-year-old executive takes charge at a crucial juncture, as Apple confronts escalating market pressure to match competitors in the fast-moving artificial intelligence (AI) landscape.Ternus brings 25 years of experience to the chief executive role, having first arrived at Apple in 2001 as part of its design group. He has worked with Apple cofounder and former CEO Steve Jobs . He advanced to vice president in 2013 and was elevated to senior vice president of hardware engineering in 2021, reporting directly to Cook.Throughout his executive leadership, Ternus guided hardware engineering initiatives across Apple's cornerstone devices, including the iPhone, Mac, iPad, Apple Watch and Vision Pro.
Article Summary: Elon Musk, AMD CEO Lisa Su, Salesforce chief Mac Benioff, Logan Kilpatrick extend congratulations to new Apple CEO John Ternus. The 51-year-old executive takes charge at a crucial juncture as Apple confronts escalating market pressure to match competitors in the fast-moving artificial intelligence (AI) landscape.

Article Title: India's BRICS Chairship puts innovation and digital cooperation at centre stage
Article Text: India is set to put innovation, digital cooperation and inclusive technology at the centre of its BRICS agenda as it prepares to host the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on September 12-13. With the leader’s Summit approaching, India has used its BRICS Chairship to push cooperation in emerging technologies, artificial intelligence, digital public infrastructure, startups, scientific research and women’s participation in technology and entrepreneurship.The Summit will be held under the theme "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability" which is rooted in Prime Minister Narendra Modi's vision of "Humanity First".This will be India’s fourth time hosting the BRICS Summit, after it hosted the leader’s meetings in 2012, 2016 and 2021.As part of its Chairship, India has highlighted its digital public infrastructure (DPI) ecosystem, including Aadhaar and the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), as examples of affordable, scalable and inclusive digital solutions.The focus on technology has also featured in a series of Ministerial and Working-Group Meetings held during the year.The 12th BRICS Communications Ministers’ Meeting, hosted by India in August, discussed Artificial Intelligence, cloud technologies, digital governance and resilient communication networks.India has also sought to strengthen Innovation and Entrepreneurship cooperation among BRICS countries through initiatives such as the proposed BRICS Startup Innovation Fund and the BRICS Startup Innovation Network. These initiatives are aimed at creating greater opportunities for startups, investors and innovation ecosystems across member countries.Another proposal, the BRICS Science and Research Repository seeks to facilitate the sharing of research capabilities and strengthen scientific cooperation among BRICS nations.The Chairship has also given greater attention to women’s participation in technology and entrepreneurship. The BRICS Women Working Group has been working towards policy cooperation on digital inclusion and women’s entrepreneurship.The BRICS Women's Startup Contest, organized through the BRICS Women's Business Alliance, is aimed at identifying and supporting women-led ventures in sectors such as sustainability, innovation and technology.The Women in Innovation, Science and Entrepreneurship (WISE) initiative is focused on three areas– Innovation & Collaboration, Access to Funding, and Policy Advocacy. It seeks to address gender equity gaps and structural barriers that limit women’s participation and leadership in STEM and entrepreneurship.The upcoming summit is expected to provide an opportunity for BRICS leaders to discuss a common approach towards innovation in the artificial intelligence era, digital cooperation, scientific collaboration and inclusive growth.The deliberations will take place against the backdrop of rapid technological change and evolving global challenges, with member countries expected to explore ways to leverage technology and innovation to build resilient, sustainable and inclusive economies.Through its Chairship, India has sought to position BRICS as not only a platform for economic and geo-political cooperation but also as a forum for practical partnerships in emerging technologies, digital public infrastructure, startups, scientific research and inclusive innovation.
Article Summary: India is set to host the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on September 12-13. The Summit will be held under the theme "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability" The focus on technology has also featured in a series of Ministerial and Working-Group Meetings held during the year.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Bill Gates: "I really had a lot of dreams when I was a kid, and I think a great deal of that…" - how reading can expand a child's imagination and ambitions
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Bill Gates (PTI photo)

Quote of the day by Bill Gates

"I really had a lot of dreams when I was a kid, and I think a great deal of that grew out of the fact that I had a chance to read a lot"

What did Bill Gates actually mean by this quote

Why this quote still genuinely matters today

How books can genuinely expand a child's imagination

Reading can genuinely turn curiosity into real ambition

Bill Gates and his own childhood interest in computers

The genuine connection between reading and lifelong learning

Other famous quotes by Bill Gates

"Be nice to nerds. Chances are you'll end up working for one."

"If you give people tools, and they use their natural abilities and their curiosity, they will develop things in ways that will surprise you very much beyond what you might have expected."

"I'd be happy if I could think that the role of the library was sustained and even enhanced in the age of the computer."

"Your most unhappy customers are your greatest source of learning."

How to apply this quote by Bill Gates in daily life

Why this quote by Bill Gates remains relevant today

For many children, reading begins as something genuinely simple, a way to pass time, complete a school assignment, or escape into a fictional world for an hour. It can also quietly shape how a child actually thinks, imagines, and understands what might genuinely be possible for their own life. Bill Gates said this directly in a 2002 Livewire interview, an online interview series that let users submit questions in real time. "I really had a lot of dreams when I was a kid," he said, "and I think a great deal of that grew out of the fact that I had a chance to read a lot." He connects his own early habit of reading directly with the genuinely large ambitions he developed while still young. The idea is genuinely simple but powerful, that what children actually read can expand the world they honestly believe is available to them. Books can introduce unfamiliar places, careers, cultures, and ideas long before children encounter them through their own experiences.Gates is suggesting that reading gave him real access to ideas well beyond his immediate surroundings. As a child, a person's understanding of the world is naturally limited to what they actually see and experience directly. Books can dramatically widen that picture. A child can genuinely read about ancient civilisations, distant planets or computers without ever actually leaving home, and that exposure can genuinely change how a young person thinks about their own future.When Gates says his dreams "grew out of" having the chance to read widely, he is describing reading as a real source of possibility. Books gave him information, but they also gave him actual ideas about what people could genuinely achieve. The word "chance" genuinely matters too. Gates recognised that having access to books was itself a real advantage, since not every child grows up with the same access to libraries or a genuinely supportive learning environment.Children today genuinely have access to more information than any previous generation, with a smartphone providing articles and digital libraries within seconds. Access to information, though, is not necessarily the same thing as deep, genuine reading. A short video is designed to capture attention quickly. A book asks a reader to stay with an idea over a genuinely longer period, following an argument or imagining a world properly. Gates' quote remains relevant because imagination still genuinely needs real material to work with. A child cannot dream about becoming an astronaut without first actually learning that space exploration exists in the first place, and reading can provide exactly that first genuine spark.A book can take a child considerably beyond their immediate environment. Someone growing up far from the ocean can genuinely read about marine life, and a student interested in history can learn about societies that existed thousands of years ago. Fiction does something genuinely similar in a different way, encouraging readers to imagine characters and situations that do not actually exist in front of them. That process can genuinely strengthen a child's ability to imagine real alternatives, helping them understand that the world can actually be different from what they currently see around them. This matters because many real ambitions genuinely begin as imagined possibilities long before they become anything concrete.Curiosity often genuinely begins with a simple question. Why does the Moon look different some nights? How does a computer actually work? Reading can provide some real answers while creating even more questions in the process, and that cycle is genuinely valuable, since one book can lead directly to another. Gates' own childhood reading was genuinely part of this process, and his interest in computers eventually became considerably more than a passing childhood fascination, contributing directly to the path that led him to co-found Microsoft. Reading alone never guarantees genuine success on its own. It can, though, give people real ideas and curiosity that genuinely influence the direction they eventually take.Bill Gates was born in Seattle, Washington, in 1955, and developed a genuine interest in computing while still a school student, gaining access to computers at a time when they were considerably less common than they are today. His curiosity eventually led him to spend real time learning about programming, and while studying at Harvard University, he and his childhood friend Paul Allen became increasingly focused on the emerging personal-computer industry. In 1975, Gates and Allen founded Microsoft, which went on to become one of the world's most influential technology companies. Gates later became known not only for his work in technology but also for genuine philanthropy through the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, supporting work in global health, education and scientific research.Gates' quote also carries relevance well beyond childhood. Adults can genuinely fall into the habit of believing that real learning happens primarily in school or university. In reality, reading can remain one of the simplest ways to genuinely continue learning throughout an entire life. Gates himself has said elsewhere that he would be genuinely happy to think the role of the library "was sustained and even enhanced in the age of the computer," a sentiment that fits closely with today's quote about the actual value of reading widely.The simplest way to apply Gates' message is to genuinely make reading a regular part of life, without needing to read several books every month. Even a genuinely small amount of consistent reading can expose someone to real new ideas. Parents can build a genuine reading routine at home by keeping books easily available and letting children choose whatever genuinely interests them. Adults can set aside a few minutes each day for a book rather than relying entirely on short digital content, and it genuinely helps to read across different subjects too. If you normally read fiction, try a real biography instead. The goal was never simply to finish more books. It is to actually encounter ideas that make you think genuinely differently.Bill Gates' quote about childhood dreams and reading is ultimately a reminder of how genuinely powerful exposure to ideas can actually be. Books do considerably more than provide information. They can introduce a child to people and possibilities that exist well beyond their immediate surroundings, and those ideas can genuinely spark real questions, which can eventually become genuine interests, skills and ambitions. Gates credits much of his own childhood dreaming to having the genuine opportunity to read widely, and his experience does not mean every child who reads will become a technology entrepreneur. It does suggest something considerably simpler though, that when people genuinely have access to ideas, they have more real possibilities to imagine for themselves. Sometimes a genuine dream really does begin with something as ordinary as opening a book.
Article Summary: Bill Gates was born in Seattle, Washington, in 1955. He developed a genuine interest in computing while still a school student. His interest in computers eventually led him to co-found Microsoft. Gates said his dreams "grew out of" having the chance to read widely.

Article Title: 'You have 18 days and 44 minutes': US brewery's message to the thief who stole its truckload of beer
Article Text:
Image source: Twitter

Reason behind the unusual '18 days and 44 minutes' deadline

How the beer theft happened

A US beer company has given a thief 18 days and 44 minutes to return a truckload of stolen beer. According to a BBC report, Pabst Brewing Company said around 40,000 pounds (18,144kg) of Pabst Blue Ribbon beer, worth about $25,000, was stolen from a distribution centre in California after someone allegedly used fake documents to collect the shipment. The company has now turned to social media to try to find the missing beer. "Pabst is officially starting the clock now - you have exactly 18 days and 44 minutes to return our truckload of beer, no questions asked," the company said in the post.The unusual deadline is not random. Pabst was founded in 1844, which is why the company chose 18 days and 44 minutes.Pabst said the incident may sound unusual, but stressed that the theft is real. “We realise how ridiculous that sounds, but it's the truth,” the company said in its social media post. “This is real and we are deadly serious.”Pabst also joked about the thief wanting to show off the amount of PBR they had. “STOLEN,” the company announced. “To the thief: we don't fault you for wanting to brag to your friends how much PBR you have, we just wish you obtained it the honourable way.”The brewery also offered an unspecified reward for information that helps recover the shipment.The stolen beer was being held at an Anheuser-Busch distribution centre in Montclair, California, and was supposed to be delivered to San Diego. According to Montclair police, the alleged thief arrived at the facility with fraudulent paperwork and managed to collect the shipment.A spokesperson said the person who collected the beer was not the driver or person who was supposed to pick up the shipment.“What we discovered was it was just a bad actor essentially who came in and pretended to be the person who was supposed to pick up the beer,” the spokesperson told CBS News.“It wasn't the person who was supposed to pick up the beer and then they drove off with it.”Police said another shipment worth around $45,000 and headed for Tucson, Arizona, was picked up earlier on 17 August. However, it had still not reached its destination two weeks later. About an hour after that incident, the shipment of Pabst Blue Ribbon beer was collected using fraudulent documents.Police are investigating whether the two incidents were connected. “Investigators identified similarities between the two incidents,” police said. “Information provided regarding the trucking company, driver and vehicles involved contained discrepancies and is currently being investigated.”
Article Summary: 40,000 pounds (18,144kg) of Pabst Blue Ribbon beer, worth about $25,000, was stolen from a distribution centre in California. The company has now turned to social media to try to find the missing beer.

Article Title: Tim Cook made Apple unshakeable, now John Ternus has to shake it
Article Text:
Tim Cook hands Apple to John Ternus after 15 years, with the hard problems intact

Cook's Apple was built to survive, not to surprise

Ternus builds things, which is the whole reason he has the job

Cook is staying because Ternus needs him to

Next week will not tell you much

There is an office at Apple 's old Infinite Loop campus that has been locked and dark since 2011. It was Steve Jobs 's, and when Tim Cook took over he never moved into it. Fifteen years later, nobody has.John Ternus is expected to take Cook's office at Apple Park. Cook kept his distance from the man he replaced and spent fifteen years being compared to him anyway. Ternus starts at Cook's desk, with Cook down the hall. He is staying on as executive chairman, has told colleagues he will keep running Washington and Beijing himself, and said as much in the note he sent staff on his last day in the job: he is not leaving Apple, he is stepping away from a role he loved.Every part of that is sensible. It also means the person who has spent fifteen years setting Apple's instincts is still there while the new man tries to change them.Consider what he inherited in August 2011. Jobs had spent a decade making wagers that could have finished the company and kept winning them: the iMac, the iPod, a phone with no keyboard, a tablet nobody had asked for. That was the house style.Cook did something else. He looked at the iPhone, understood what it was worth, and spent fifteen years building a world around it so that leaving became unthinkable.The Watch in 2014, AirPods in 2016, then Apple Pay, Apple Music, iCloud and the App Store, each one charging a little every month. The services business he assembled out of that now earns more than all of Apple did on the day he started. Revenue roughly quadrupled to $416 billion, market value rose fifteenfold past $4.7 trillion, and there are now more than 2.5 billion active Apple devices in the world against a few hundred million when he arrived.None of it came from a product. It came from operations, which is what Cook had been doing since 1998. He knew what every component cost and where it came from, and he squeezed until the margins moved. Dropping Intel for Apple's own silicon took gross margins from about 40 per cent in 2011 to nearly 50 per cent today, which is the most consequential decision of his tenure and one you have never seen or been sold.He did swing occasionally, and it kept not landing. The Vision Pro was his, championed as the device that would make computing spatial and eventually succeed the phone, and it has ended up an expensive object for enthusiasts, with jobs now being cut across the programme. The iPhone Air was a new shape for the product that pays for everything and did not find its buyers. The car ran for a decade and several billion dollars before it was shut in 2024.What the operations work bought was a company that cannot be knocked over. Maps launched badly in 2012, he apologised in writing, the iPhone did not blink. Tariffs took $638 billion off Apple's value in three days last April and it came back within weeks. The EU took $14.4 billion in back taxes and about $4 billion more in fines, the US justice department sued over monopoly claims, App Store commissions were forced down in several markets and rival app stores prised open in Europe. Margins went up through all of it.That durability has a cost, and AI is where it showed up. Cook's method had never failed before: turn up late, turn up finished. Apple did not invent the MP3 player, the smartphone, the tablet, the smartwatch or wireless earbuds. It let someone else prove a category, then walked in with better hardware and better margins. AI did not wait. Apple Intelligence stumbled at launch in 2024, the Siri overhaul slipped by nearly two years, the acquisition Apple went shopping for never happened, and Cook removed the AI chief and reassigned the executive running Siri. Last year Apple gave up on its own models and started paying Google to put Gemini underneath Siri.Cook's memo describes the pattern without meaning to. The thing he says he is proudest of is what an annual report could never capture, that culture beats everything else. He is right, and it is the most revealing line in the letter. He built a culture, not a product, and cultures are magnificent at continuing to be themselves.He is Apple's first chief executive in three decades to have spent his career on hardware, and that is the argument for him.He joined in 2001, after a mechanical engineering degree from Penn, where he swam varsity, and four years designing headsets at a virtual reality startup. His first work at Apple was on screens for Macs. By 2005 he was leading hardware engineering for the iMac G5, where his team wanted to hold the glass in place with magnets, an idea treated as odd at the time and one he pushed through anyway. Promoted to manager, he was offered an office and turned it down twice, staying in open seating with his team. He spent long stretches in Asia learning how hard it is to make a supplier deliver what a designer drew.His first note to staff was mostly thanks, which is what a first note to staff always is. What is interesting is where it ends. Not on the launch he calls phenomenal, but on what sits behind it, the products already in the works and the ones nobody has imagined yet. Cook's letters were about the team and the values. Ternus wrote his about the pipeline.Then there is the other Ternus. Around 2018, Apple weighed putting a small laser in the iPhone for better photos and mapping, at about $40 a device. Ternus, running hardware, proposed putting it only in the Pro models, on the reasoning that the loyalists would pay for new technology and nobody else would notice. Commercially it was the right call. It is also the reflex that kept Apple out of the AI race, and it now belongs to the chief executive. Six former employees have described him as better known for maintaining products than creating them. One former engineering manager put it more bluntly than anyone inside would like: if you want to make an iPhone every year, Ternus is your guy.He has been willing to say no to Cook's projects, though. He never accepted the Vision Pro argument, on the grounds that it was too heavy and too expensive to go mainstream, and Apple has been cutting that programme since he was elevated. He backs the smart glasses instead, and is said to be open to leaving head-worn devices altogether if they do not take.Start with what he already has. The foldable iPhone next week, the first genuinely new shape the product has taken. A 20th anniversary iPhone in 2027. Then the things still some way off: smart glasses next year, AirPods with cameras that read your surroundings, a home display on a robotic arm, a wearable pendant, a touchscreen MacBook. All of it approved by Ternus as hardware chief, all of it the "already in the works" half of his memo, and more new hardware than Cook shipped in fifteen years. The other half, the products nobody has imagined yet, is the part that has to come from the new job.The difficulty is everything around the products. He is thin on finance, legal, procurement and government relations, which is most of a modern chief executive's week. Cook keeps Washington and Beijing, and has been personally working through the memory shortage that has already pushed up MacBook and iPad prices, with iPhones expected next. Analysts have started asking whether Apple's growth this year is coming from volume or from price.He also inherits a supply chain that exists in its current form only because an operations man built it. India assembles roughly a quarter of Apple's global iPhones now, about 55 million units in 2025, and the entire iPhone 17 line was made here before launch. Vietnam took AirPods, iPads and Watches. A small US assembly base was set up largely to satisfy Donald Trump, with a $600 billion investment pledge attached and promises of more. None of it was visionary. All of it was necessary, and it is now Ternus's to keep running while he tries to do something else.The bench is emptying at the same time. Jeff Williams, the chief operating officer long assumed to be the natural successor, retired in December after 27 years. Luca Maestri, finance chief for a decade, has moved into a smaller role. Phil Schiller gave up the App Store and Apple's product events days before the handover, which colleagues read as a step towards retiring outright, and he is the last visible link to the Jobs era. Roughly half the leadership team could be gone within a few years. Below them, engineers have been leaving for Meta and for OpenAI's hardware division, which Apple is now suing over trade secrets.So the pipeline says risk-taker and the record says careful, and Cook is still in the building.Ternus stands on that stage next week while Cook sits in the room, off it for the first time in fifteen years. The wider Siri rollout lands the same week, which means his first month contains both the thing he built and the thing he inherited.The foldable will tell you nothing. A folding iPhone seven years after Samsung is what turning up late and finished looks like, and it would have shipped under Cook too. Watch for something duller: whether this company, under a product man, puts real money into something that does not pay for itself inside a product cycle, and whether a board that has enjoyed fifteen years without a bad quarter will sit through one while he tries.Signing out, Cook wrote that Apple made its dent in the universe because of what it values and how it sees the world. He meant it as a description of a culture built to endure, which it is. That is the inheritance and the problem in the same sentence. Cook spent fifteen years making Apple a company that nothing could knock over. Ternus now has to find out what it can build if it lets itself be knocked.
Article Summary: John Ternus is expected to take Cook's office at Apple Park. Cook kept his distance from the man he replaced and spent fifteen years being compared to him anyway. Cook's method had never failed before: turn up late, turn up finished. Apple did not invent the MP3 player, the smartphone, the tablet, the smartwatch or wireless earbuds.

Article Title: Sam Altman to everyone opposing data centers: They suffer from 'reputation problem' and not 'water problem'
Article Text:
OpenAI CEO Sam ​Altman

Why water has become a flashpoint in the AI backlash

The Almond comparison

Altman's Prescription: Deliver value, not arguments

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has now dismissed the concerns about AI’s water consumption, calling it a ‘meme’ that doesn’t hold up under scrutiny. According to a report by Business Insider, speaking on the premiere episode of Alex Heath’s Sources Podcast, Altman argued that while data centers have a reputation for being water guzzlers, most modern facilities use about as much water as a large office building. Altman's claim has some real backing. A 2024 report from a Virginia state government commission — Virginia being a major data center hub — found that while water usage varied significantly between individual facilities, most data centers consumed about the same amount of water as an average large office building, or less.Water consumption has emerged as a central concern in the broader public pushback against data center construction. A Gallup report published in May found that 71% of Americans opposed building a data center in their own area, with 70% specifically citing concerns about environmental impact. Half of respondents pointed to effects on local resources generally, and 18% named water specifically as a concern.That concern isn't entirely without basis. A Business Insider investigation published last year found that data centers were contributing to worsening water scarcity in parts of the western United States, driven in part by water-intensive evaporative cooling systems used to keep servers from overheating.The Data Center Coalition, an industry trade group, has said developers use a range of cooling approaches, including some closed-loop or fully waterless systems, and that the industry prioritizes water efficiency tailored to local water availability.To illustrate his point, Altman compared ChatGPT's water usage to that of growing almonds in California, a notoriously water-intensive crop. He said producing a single California almond requires more water than is used across thousands of ChatGPT queries combined, adding that people eating a handful of almonds generally don't feel like they're doing anything environmentally harmful.Business Insider said it could not independently verify Altman's exact comparison, but noted the broader claim roughly lines up with available data. Altman has previously stated that an average ChatGPT query uses about 0.32 milliliters of water, while Google has said an average Gemini app text prompt uses roughly 0.26 milliliters. By comparison, a 2019 study involving researchers affiliated with the U.S. Geological Survey found that growing a single almond in California requires an average of 3.56 liters of water — just under a gallon per nut.Despite dismissing the substance of the water concerns, Altman said he believes it's the AI industry's job to actively change public perception rather than simply insist the criticism is misplaced. He said the most effective way to get people to embrace something is by delivering them real value, and acknowledged that the industry still has work to do in making AI products easier to use and easier for people to genuinely benefit from.
Article Summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has dismissed the concerns about AI’s water consumption, calling it a ‘meme’ that doesn’t hold up under scrutiny. Altman argued that while data centers have a reputation for being water guzzlers, most modern facilities use about as much water as a large office building.
